overview: This bill, the PORCUPINE Act, puts Taiwan on the same footing as close U.S. allies under the Arms Export Control Act, the law that governs U.S. weapons sales abroad. Under current law, sales to NATO members, Japan, Australia, South Korea, Israel, and New Zealand get shorter congressional review periods and higher dollar thresholds before Congress must be notified; the bill adds Taiwan to that list, which would speed up approval of arms sales to Taiwan. It also orders the State Department to study, within 90 days, whether it could fast-track approvals when those allies want to transfer U.S.-origin military equipment to Taiwan, including possible 15- and 30-day deadlines for decisions. The bill states it does not change long-standing U.S. policy toward Taiwan under the Taiwan Relations Act, and it expires after seven years. The Senate passed it on December 11, 2025, and as of December 15, 2025, it was awaiting action in the House.
for: Supporters say treating Taiwan like other close partners cuts delays in getting it the equipment it needs to deter an attack, at a time when tensions with China are high.
against: Critics say shortening the review periods gives Congress less time to scrutinize weapons sales, and that faster arms transfers to Taiwan could raise tensions with China.
